food.text: Bars of rock salt called Amolé were mined in the Afar depression and used instead of money throughout the highlands. The salt plains of Arho supplied the plateau with most of the raw salt eaten by people and their cattle.

The Ajuran Sultanate was Africa's only 'hydraulic empire' by the 15th century. Irrigation ditches called Kelliyo carried water from the Shebelle and Jubba rivers into plantations growing sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton.

Fourteenth-century texts said the people of the Zeila region were fond of the stimulant khat leaf, which was grown locally. One of the earliest textual references to coffee also comes from the Zeila region, where a scholar wrote about its development from a tree.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has 250 fasting days, 180 of which are obligatory for lay people, not just monks and priests. On fast days adherents abstain from meat and animal products, eating only vegan food, and they also refrain from sexual activity. During the 40-day Advent fast only one vegan meal is allowed per day.

In the southern Ethiopian Highlands lay the Kingdom of Kaffa, a medieval and early modern state from which the coffee plant was exported to the Arabian Peninsula. Its fertile land could produce three harvests a year, and the word coffee, from Arabic qahwah, is traced to Kaffa.
Jewish merchants from Hormuz brought Indian textiles and fruits to the Somali coast. In exchange they took away grain and wood.

Duarte Barbosa noted an abundance of meat, wheat, barley, horses and fruit in the coastal markets of the Ajuran lands. He wrote that this abundance generated enormous wealth for the merchants. Ships from the Kingdom of Cambaya brought cloths and spices and received gold, wax and ivory.

Farmers in the Ajuran lands used a land measurement system to determine the average size of a farm. The terms used were moos, taraab and guldeed. Farms in Afgooye, Kismayo and other areas became more productive under central supervision.

The Afar port of Beilul was visited by Arab ships from Mocha and Aden, which took on provisions of corn, butter and honey. They also took tusks, cow-hides and civet, along with a few slaves, all brought down from the highlands. The goods were exchanged for spices, pepper and broadcloth.

Traders in the Afar lowlands once earned their king's revenue chiefly by furnishing camels for carrying goods from the interior, when trade with India flourished. By James Bruce's day, trade was in decline and largely confined to hauling bars of rock salt through "dry and burning deserts". The carriers ran great risk of being murdered by the Galla before reaching the nearest highland market, and earned only "a moderate profit".
One of the earliest textual references to coffee describes its development from a tree in the Zeila region. The beverage is believed to have spread from Adal to the Rasulids in the fifteenth century.

In 1542, a Portuguese crew captured a ship from Zeila that was carrying clarified butter and coffee to Al-Shihr. The coffee beverage is believed to have spread from Adal to the Rasulids in the fifteenth century.

art.text: Lalibela is famous for its rock-cut monolithic churches, which are traditionally dated to the reign of the Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela (r. c. 1181–1221). The rock-hewn churches were declared a World Heritage Site in 1978. To some Christians, the town is one of Ethiopia's holiest cities and a center of pilgrimage.

Aksumite stelae and later entire churches were carved from single blocks of rock, and this tradition was emulated at Lalibela and throughout Tigray. Rock-cut building was concentrated in Tigray in the 10th and 11th centuries and mainly around Lalibela in the 12th century.

Vasco da Gama, passing Mogadishu in the 15th century, noted a large city with houses four or five storeys high and big palaces at its centre. He also saw many mosques with cylindrical minarets. Ibn Battuta described Mogadishu and Zeila as one country, a journey between them taking him eight weeks.
The Zagwe dynasty, established in the 12th century, built churches out of solid rock. These rock-hewn structures include the Church of St. George at Lalibela.

The Church of Saint George was carved downwards from volcanic tuff, which was the sole architectural material used in the structure. It is among the best known and last built of the eleven churches, and has been called the Eighth Wonder of the World.

The layout and names of the major buildings in Lalibela are widely accepted, especially by local clergy, to be a symbolic representation of Jerusalem. This has led some experts to date the current church construction to the years following the capture of Jerusalem in 1187 by Saladin.
Emperor Zara Yaqob (1434–1468) led the Ethiopian Empire to its peak. Among his achievements, he built numerous churches and monasteries and encouraged literature and art.

The Fakr ad-Din mosque in Mogadishu dates to 1269 and was built by and named after the first Sultan of the Mogadishu Sultanate. Made of marble and coral stone, it has a domed mihrab decorated with glazed tiles, one of which bears a dated inscription. Its design is not replicated in mosques further south outside the Horn region.

Carving Lalibela's churches from living rock must have taken longer than the few decades of King Gebre Meskel Lalibela's reign. David Roden Buxton therefore assumed the work extended into the 14th century.

Kilwa's Great Mosque was built from square coral limestone blocks, with three symmetrical entrances with vaulted ceilings. Uniquely for mosques in the area, its flat roof was supported by nine hexagonal columns made from single tree trunks.
Kilwa's Great Mosque is one of the first mosques built without a sahn. Its northern prayer hall had 16 bays supported by nine pillars, originally carved from coral but later replaced by timber.

According to local tradition, Gebre Meskel Lalibela was guided by Jesus on a tour of Jerusalem before he took the throne, and was told to build a second Jerusalem in Ethiopia. Lalibela, traditionally known as Roha, was founded under the Zagwe dynasty. It is more likely, though, that the churches evolved over several phases of construction and alteration of earlier structures.

Most Aksumite-style structures, such as palaces, villas and monasteries, were built of alternating layers of stone and wood. The protruding wooden support beams are called "monkey heads". The 12th-century monastery of Yemrehanna Krestos near Lalibela was built in this style during the Zagwe dynasty.
Rock-hewn churches were not limited to the north of Ethiopia. Adadi Mariam, dating to the 15th century, lies about 100 km south of Addis Ababa, showing how far the tradition spread.

Mogadishu was the center of a thriving weaving industry known as toob benadir, which was specialized for the markets in Egypt and Syria. Together with Merca and Barawa, it also served as a transit stop for Swahili merchants from Mombasa and Malindi.
The Church of Saint George stands in an artificial trench, with a small baptismal pool outside the church. The trench measures 25 meters by 25 meters by 30 meters.

Around 1331, the traveller Ibn Battuta described a grand dome at Kilwa's Great Mosque, added in the early 14th century by Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman. He claimed the mosque was entirely wooden, but stone walls were found to predate the fourteenth century.

Recent excavations at Lalibela have yielded abundant pottery and faunal remains dating to 900–1100, suggesting the site was largely a secular settlement before King Lalibela turned it into a religious center. Near it, the Washa Mikael cave has prechristian carved animal friezes on its lower walls, with Christian paintings later added to the upper walls.

For centuries, Arba'a Rukun (1269) and Fakr ad-Din (1269) were among the only mosques in East Africa with minarets. Arba Rukun's massive round coral tower is about 13.5 meters high, and its doorway is surrounded by multiple recessed arches. This may be the first example of the recessed arch that became a prototype for the local mihrab style.

Between 1294 and 1302, Kilwa's Great Mosque was extended southward with a semicircular vault where the sultan prayed. The extension had square bays divided by a space in between, leaving no central court.

war.text: In 1270, Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty and founded the Ethiopian Empire and its Solomonic dynasty. He claimed descent from the last Aksumite king and ultimately from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, while later church texts accused the Zagwe of lacking pure Solomonic stock.

The Ethiopian Empire grew through the crusades of Amda Seyon I (1314–1344) and Dawit I (1382–1413), temporarily becoming the dominant force in the Horn of Africa. Amda Seyon invaded the Sultanate of Ifat, killing the sultan, sacking the capital and ravaging the Muslim territories: his army took livestock, killed many inhabitants, destroyed towns and mosques, and took slaves. Dawit I's army defeated Ifat, besieged and captured Zeila and killed Sultan Sa'ad ad-Din, ending the sultanate, and the Amhara then made churches from the ravaged mosques. Zara Yaqob (1434–1468) then consolidated these conquests and expanded his hegemony over adjacent Islamic territories.

Soldiers in medieval Ethiopia universally used the sword and spear, and cavalry were often equipped with chain mail and helmets. The bow and arrow were widespread, and arrow poison was occasionally used. Ifat forces also used the javelin and the shotel.

Yekuno Amlak's victory at Ansata in 1270 was helped by outside allies. The Gafat, six regiments under a Christian supporter named Mālēzāy, and Sultan Dil Gamis of the Sultanate of Shewa all backed him, giving the Amhara rebels an advantage over the Zagwe. After defeating the Zagwe army, he chased the king Yetbarak into the church of Saint Qirqos at Ansata and killed him there.

Emperor Yeshaq I spent much of his reign defending his eastern territories from Muslim harassment. He seems to have used Egyptian Christian advisors to drill his army and teach them to make Greek fire. It was not enough, and he was killed fighting the Adalites in 1429.

During Amda Seyon's invasion of the Ifat Sultanate in the fourteenth century, the state of Mora joined a coalition with Adal and elected Imam Salih as their leader. Mora was also among the states an Abyssinian emperor referred to when describing raids carried out in his realm purely to capture slaves, meaning people there were seized and enslaved.

After Yeshaq's death in 1429, five emperors succeeded one another in five years before Zara Yaqob took the throne in 1434. The Walashma had returned from exile in 1415 and founded the Adal Sultanate around the Harar region.

In the mid-fourteenth century, the Ifat leader Jamal ad-Din I rebelled against Abyssinia by allying with the Adal leader Salih to fight the forces of Emperor Amda Seyon. Later, the rebel leaders Haqq ad-Din II and Sa'ad ad-Din II moved their base to Adal in the Harar region, founding the Adal Sultanate.

In 1445, following the Battle of Gomit, chronicles record that Emperor Zara Yaqob began garrisoning the provinces with Chewa regiments, after repelling an Adal invasion of the Dawaro province and killing the Adalite Sultan Badlay.

literature.text: After the Aksumites declined, no Ethiopian works survive that can be dated to the 8th through 12th centuries. Only with the rise of the Solomonic dynasty around 1270 is there evidence of authors committing their works to writing. Some writers consider the period from the 14th century a "Golden Age" of Ge'ez literature.

By the time of the Golden Age, Ge'ez was no longer a living language, having been replaced by Amharic in the south and by Tigrigna and Tigre in the north. It nonetheless remained the official written language until the 19th century. Its status was comparable to that of Medieval Latin in Europe.

The Kebra Nagast, a 14th-century national epic, describes the Solomonic dynasty's claim to descent from Solomon. It states that Aksum was founded by Menelik I, allegedly the son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. The epic was used to justify the takeover from the Zagwe dynasty.

Literature flourished especially during the reign of Emperor Zara Yaqob. He himself wrote Mats'hafe Berhan ("The Book of Light") and Mats'hafe Milad ("The Book of Nativity"). Numerous homilies were also written in this period.

According to the Kebra Nagast, written in Ge'ez in 1321, Menelik I was conceived when Solomon tricked the visiting Queen of Sheba into sleeping with him. Menelik was raised Jewish in his mother's homeland and first traveled to Jerusalem in his twenties. One account says Menelik and his companions took the Ark of the Covenant home with them.

The royal biographical genre was established during the reign of Amda Seyon I, who ruled from 1314 to 1344. His chronicle, The Glorious Victories of Amda Seyon, is far more detailed than any earlier Ethiopian history. Historian Richard Pankhurst called it a "masterpiece in historical chronicling".

A Ge'ez translation of the Fetha Negest ("Laws of the Kings") is thought to have been made around 1450 and is ascribed to Petros Abda Sayd. It later served as the supreme law of Ethiopia until a modern Constitution replaced it in 1931.

The History of Alexander, believed to have been written around 1500, narrates the life and conquests of Alexander the Great. It depicts him as a Christian warrior. Another significant text is the travel account of Takla 'Alfa, an Ethiopian monk who visited the city of Old Dongola.

A panegyric addressed to Emperor Yeshaq I, who reigned from 1414 to 1429/1430, survives as a notable example of Ethiopian literature. Enrico Cerulli singled it out as a gem of Ethiopian poetry. Yeshaq's victory song also contains the first mention of the Yem people, who are said to pay tribute in horses.

The first mention of the ethnonym "Somali" dates to the reign of Emperor Yishaq. He had one of his court officials compose a hymn celebrating a military victory over the Sultan of Ifat and his troops.

The Sirat Sayf ibn Dhi-Yazan is a 15th century Arabic epic set during the Axumite conquest of Yemen. Its principal antagonist, Sayf Ar'ed, was likely inspired by the Ethiopian emperor and helped date the work. Jean-Claude Garcin says it was triggered by Yeshaq I's capture of Zeila in 1415.

The Life of Iyasus Mo'a and the Be'ela nagastat tell of a rooster that was heard prophesying outside Yekuno Amlak's house for three months that whoever ate its head would be king. The bird was then killed and cooked, but the cook discarded the rooster's head, and Yekuno Amlak ate it and so became ruler of Ethiopia. Scholars have pointed out the similarity to a legend about the first king of Kaffa, who likewise learned from a mysterious voice that eating the head of a certain rooster would make him king.

science.text: By the 15th century the Ajuran Sultanate of the Horn of Africa was Africa's only 'hydraulic empire'. As a water dynasty, its state monopolized the water resources of the Shebelle and Jubba rivers.
Through hydraulic engineering, the Ajuran state constructed many limestone wells and cisterns. Many of them remain in use to this day.
Merchants of the Ajuran Empire did brisk business using commercial vessels and multiple port cities. Their trade reached traders in the Near East, East Asia and the wider world.

politics.text: Around 1270, Yekuno Amlak overthrew the last Zagwe king and founded the Solomonic dynasty. He claimed descent from the last Aksumite king and ultimately from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. The dynasty would rule Ethiopia until 1974.

The Ethiopian Empire reached its peak under Emperor Zara Yaqob, who reigned from 1434 to 1468. He centralized imperial authority by replacing regional warlords with administrative officials, and he expanded his hegemony over adjacent Islamic territories. He also persecuted those who admitted to worshipping pagan gods, and many of them were decapitated in public.

Ethiopia's medieval rulers developed ways to control succession. One was to intern all of the emperor's possible rivals in a secure location, which drastically limited their ability to disrupt the empire with revolts or to dispute an heir apparent's succession. Later tradition called this place the Mountain of the Princes. These royal rivals were imprisoned there, and one tradition says the 10th-century queen Yodit or "Gudit" captured Debre Damo and isolated 200 princes there to death, though the abbot of the monastery there knew of no such tale.

Emperor Zara Yaqob reigned from 1434 to 1468 and brought the Ethiopian Empire to its peak. He built numerous churches and monasteries, encouraged literature and art, and centralized imperial authority. He also launched a campaign against pagan worship and "un-Christian practices" within the church, and persecuted those who admitted to worshipping pagan gods. Many of them were decapitated in public.

The Kebra Nagast, a 14th-century national epic, described the Solomonic dynasty's claimed descent from Solomon. It was used to justify the takeover from the Zagwe dynasty. Connecting Yekuno Amlak to Menelik I gave him authority to rule, while the Cushitic Zagwe kings were denounced as illegitimate.

The Zagwe dynasty ruled northern Ethiopia and Eritrea from about 1137 to 1270. It ended when Yekuno Amlak pursued the last Zagwe king, Za-Ilmaknun, and killed him at the Battle of Ansata. His real name is lost; Za-Ilmaknun is a pseudonym the victorious Solomonic rulers used soon after his reign in an act of damnatio memoriae. The Zagwe are best known for King Lalibela, credited with ordering the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela.

In 1332 the Sultan of Ifat, Haqq ad-Din I, was slain in a campaign against Emperor Amda Seyon's troops. Amda Seyon then appointed Jamal ad-Din as the new king, followed by Jamal ad-Din's brother Nasr ad-Din.

Wedem Arad sent an envoy to Spain in 1306 to seek a religious alliance. Ethiopian monks took part in the Council of Constance in 1414 to 1418. Several diplomatic missions went from Ethiopia to Spain and Italy during the 15th century.
Taddesse Tamrat argues that under the Zagwe dynasty, succession passed from brother to brother, following Agaw laws of inheritance. This differed from the practice of later Ethiopian rulers.

After much struggle, Ifat's troops were defeated by the invading Abyssinians, and Sa'ad ad-Din II, the last Sultan of Ifat, fled to Zeila in 1403. Abyssinian forces pursued him there and slew him. His children escaped to Yemen and returned to the Harar plateau in 1415, where his eldest son, Sabr ad-Din III, set up a new base in Dakkar.
The Ajuran rulers developed new systems for agriculture and taxation. These systems continued to be used in parts of the Horn of Africa as late as the 19th century.

Fatagar was a province that separated Muslim and Christian dominions. According to one chronicle, the reputation of its ruler Ras Amdu of Wej was enough to dissuade the Abyssinians from invading, so they plotted to spread a rumour that the King slept with Queen Eleni. Amdu was furious and led an army from Wej, invading Fatagar and several other kingdoms and decisively defeating the Muslims. King Eskender then came to support the Muslims, captured Amdu and killed him. Amdu's nephew Welde Sulis succeeded him and, when he met Eskender, swore an oath not to spare him.

Taddesse Tamrat noted the 1063 death of Queen Badit as the first historically verifiable tradition of Muslims in eastern Shewa. This was more than a century after the Shewa sultanate's chronicle claimed it was founded. He placed it in a long tradition of Christian domination in the region.

French archaeologists found ruined towns near the Awash River in 2007, including Awfāt, identified as the capital of the former Ifat state. The ruins, dated to the 14th and 15th centuries, included a mosque, a water reservoir, and a necropolis for the Walashma Dynasty. At the nearby towns of Asbari and Nora, access to the housing was enclosed by walls.

philosophy.text: Ethiopian philosophy was preserved through oral tradition and, from early on, in written Ge'ez manuscripts. It covers the territories of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. It occupies a unique position within African philosophy.

Ethiopian thinkers mostly reflected on morality from a religious starting point. They preferred narrative, parable, apothegm and rich imagery to abstract argument, so wisdom was taught through stories and sayings rather than formal reasoning.

Ethiopia's wisdom literature grew from translations and adaptations of Greek texts. One of them, The Life and Maxims of Skendes, dates to the 11th century, making it an early example of foreign philosophy being reshaped in Ge'ez.

Ethiopian religious literature came from a twofold creative assimilation. Orthodoxy was tuned to traditional modes of thought that were never eradicated, and Greek pagan and early Patristic thought was absorbed into an Ethiopian-Christian synthesis.

The Kebra Nagast, a 14th-century national epic, says Aksum was founded by Menelik I, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, known in Ethiopia as Makeda. It traced the Solomonic dynasty's descent from him and was used to justify the takeover from the Zagwe dynasty.

When Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty in 1270, the Cushitic Zagwe kings were not seen as part of the Solomonic lineage. They were denounced as illegitimate rulers, so a sacred genealogy became the test of who could rightfully rule.

A later Ethiopian philosopher's conviction that all is good for the good one is said to recall the mode of thought in the profession of faith of Emperor Zara Yaqob, the 15th-century ruler. It hints at an earlier strand of Ethiopian reflection.

culture.text: Having established itself as a Christian nation, Ethiopia spread its religion to surrounding peoples who practised traditional African religions, Judaism, and, later, Islam. Although the kingdom became secluded after Aksum declined, it still took part in European religious and diplomatic affairs in the late Middle Ages.

The Ajurans developed a very rich culture that combined Somali traditions with Islamic architecture, astronomy, and art. Most inhabitants were ethnic Somali, with Yemeni, Persian, and Turkish minorities. Somali was the most common language, while Arabic was prominent in commerce and religion.

The Shewa sultanate's chronicle reports no major conversion to Islam before the 12th century. Conversions began with the Gbbh people in 1108, and by the mid fourteenth century Islam had spread widely, including among the Argobba, Werji, Tegulat and Menz peoples.

Fatagar was a province that separated Muslim and Christian dominions in the medieval Horn of Africa. Part of the Muslim states in the eleventh century, it was later invaded by Amda Seyon I. In the 15th century it became a central district and the birthplace of the future emperors Zara Yaqob and Eskender.

Medieval Ethiopia is typically described as a feudal society. Tenant farmers formed the peasant class, with landowners, nobility, and royalty above them. Because information is scarce, what we know of Ethiopian feudalism comes mainly from the later Gondarine period.

The Argobba are widely believed to be the first people in the Horn of Africa to accept Islam collectively. They led its expansion into various regions under the Sultanate of Shewa, and the Argobba and Harla seem to have relied on each other in the Islamic period.

Ethiopia took part in European religious affairs in the late Middle Ages. Wedem Arad sent an envoy to Spain in 1306 for a religious alliance, and Ethiopian monks took part in the Council of Constance in 1414–1418.
Several engravings dating back to the 13th century show the presence of the Shewa sultanate. They are found at Chelenqo, Bate, Harla near Dire Dawa, and Munesa near Lake Langano.

After Shewa was incorporated into Ifat, the Egyptian courtier Al Umari described the Ifat Sultanate as one of the largest and richest of Ethiopia's Muslim provinces. Ifat was ruled by the Walashma dynasty from 1285 to 1415.
